Anand, you guessed the new neighbour is a doctor because he carries a black bag? Let me tell you what I did at your age.
It was Pongal, and a quiet man came to stay with my uncle for the festival. He wore glasses, read books on the veranda all day and hardly spoke. I told my whole class, "He's a professor from Madras. Must be."
My father asked me, "Sudha, how many professors live in our district? And how many farmers?" I didn't want to count. The professor story was too nice.
On the last day of Pongal, the quiet man helped my uncle yoke the bullocks faster than anyone. He grew paddy two villages away. He just liked books.

qa.a: He wore glasses, read books on the veranda all day and hardly spoke.

qa.q: Why was Sudha so sure the man was a professor?
qa.a: Sudha was excited by the neat picture of glasses and books, and it felt so right that counting how many farmers there were seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: Which question in the story could have changed Sudha's guess, and why?
qa.a: The father's question about how many professors and how many farmers live in the district, because far more farmers makes farmer the better guess.

qa.q: How might the quiet man have felt if he heard he was being called a professor?
qa.a: He might have been amused or a little puzzled, since he was a paddy farmer who simply liked books.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood guess that a quiet, bookish man must be a professor, forgetting how many more farmers there were.

I was fifteen, in Nashik. One morning a boy in my class said he'd seen a leopard behind the school canteen. He described it perfectly: the spots, the yellow eyes, a torn ear. He was a serious boy, top of the class. I believed every word, and by lunch I'd told half the school.
My grandfather asked me, "When was the last leopard seen in our part of town?" Nobody could remember one, not in fifty years. "And how many big yellow dogs live behind that canteen?" Three, at least.
I was annoyed with him. The story was so detailed.
That evening the watchman found the leopard: a big spotted street dog with a torn ear. I, Shankar, never lived it down.

Last month the college health camp ran a free screening, and my result came back flagged: "positive, further testing advised" for a rare blood condition I'd never heard of. I'm Francis, and I spent the next four nights reading about it until 3 a.m.
The leaflet called the test highly accurate. In my head that meant: accurate test, positive result, so I have it. I wrote a list of people to tell. I stopped eating properly.
My roommate Joseph dragged me to the campus doctor on Monday. She drew a grid on a notepad and explained that the condition is so rare that, even with a good test, most people who screen positive turn out not to have it. That's why there's a second test.
The second test was clear.
What stays with me is how certain I felt. The word "accurate" was so loud that I never asked how rare the thing was to begin with.

qa.a: It said 'positive, further testing advised' for a rare blood condition.

qa.q: Why was Francis so sure of having the condition?
qa.a: Francis felt terrified, and the word 'accurate' made a positive result feel certain, without any thought about how rare the condition was.

qa.q: What helped Francis, and what could Francis do differently next time?
qa.a: Seeing the campus doctor helped; next time Francis could ask a doctor to explain a result straight away instead of reading alone until 3 a.m.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt during those four nights?
qa.a: Joseph was likely worried and helpless watching Francis stop eating, which is why Joseph dragged Francis to the doctor.

Counselling note, student wellness centre. Written by Anand, counsellor.
Jaya, a first-year, came in today shaking, holding a printout from last week's campus health screening. One line was marked "reactive", for a rare condition. She had already searched online and told me, "The test is ninety-something percent accurate, so I'm ninety-something percent sick."
I listened first. She had not slept properly for three nights and had missed two classes.
I did not interpret the result; that is the doctor's job. I said that screening results for rare conditions often need a second test, and that only a doctor could explain what hers meant.
What I did next: I phoned the campus clinic while she sat with me and got her a slot that afternoon. I asked her to write down her questions, starting with: how common is this, and what does a positive screen usually mean? She left calmer, list in hand.

qa.a: One line was marked 'reactive', for a rare condition.

Wednesday, 11 p.m.
The job medical today flagged my eye test. "Possible early sign of a rare eye condition. Refer to specialist." I read that line about forty times on the bus.
By dinner I had decided I was going blind. The machine is modern. Machines don't lie. I even looked up braille classes.
Deepak found me crying on the balcony. He's studying statistics, so he drew dots on the back of an envelope: thousands of people, a tiny cluster who actually have it, and a bigger group of healthy people the machine flags by mistake. "If it's rare, most flags are false alarms," he said. "Not all. Most. That's why they send you to a specialist."
I'm still scared. But I'm less sure I'm doomed.
The appointment is Friday. Deepak's coming. I'm writing my questions now.
Trisha
